utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen, and Madam Registrar to you as well. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-02-54-R77.5-PT, in the case against Florence Hartmann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Mr. Bourdon, bonjour. I understand you wish to address me before we proceed with the initial appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURDON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You can speak in French. I can follow, although I prefer not to try to speak French because I might make mistakes. Okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURDON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I am the counsel representing Ms. Hartmann. She is now seated in a place of this courtroom where she should not be, in my view. The main mission of your Tribunal is to judge those who have been accused because of the heinous crimes they have committed against humanity. Ms. Hartmann is not charged with crimes against humanity. She is charged with contempt of the Court, and if you have a special remit regarding those that have been charged with contempt, it is a marginal competency; and it would be an understatement to say that what Ms. Hartmann is charged has anything to do with what is generally charged against the people appearing here. So I think it is perfectly normal, and it would be adequate for Ms. Hartmann, who's only charged for some kind of intellectual offence, she should not be there in a place that is usually occupied by those who have or who are alleged to have committed very serious crimes. She should be closer to her counsel. I do not insist on her sitting right next to me, but for the sake of pragmatism, as it were, and in order to make things easier, I think it would be proper for her to sit as closely as possible to me, be it next to me or behind. Mr. Macfarlane was kind enough to say that he would not oppose my motion, this oral motion I'm now presenting to you. This is the reason why, Mr. President, I may ask you now to authorise Ms. Florence Hartmann to leave the place where she is now, which is unduly offending, and for her to be seated as closely as possible to her counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourdon. Mr. Macfarlane, would you wish to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. I am Bruce MacFarlane -- Your Honour, thank you. My name is Bruce MacFarlane. I've been appointed the amicus curiae Prosecutor in this matter, and it is quite accurate to say that I have no objection to Ms. Hartmann coming forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you both. The position of the Trial Chamber or the pre-trial chamber, as far as I am concerned, is as follows. I disagree completely with you, especially in the way you've described your client's alleged responsibility. I suggest Mr. Bourdon and also, Madam Hartmann, that you to not underestimate, not even for a second, the gravity of the crime of contempt as envisaged in our setup. And I also wish to state that the power of this Tribunal to try those who are alleged or suspected of having rendered themselves culpable of contempt is an inherent right of this Tribunal and also prescribed in our Rules. However, I am on record as one of the Judges who have repeatedly criticised the distance between accused and counsel, considering the layout of these courtrooms, particularly the bigger courtrooms, Courtroom I and Courtroom III, where I have worked mostly, as against Courtroom I, which was easier; and I have always advocated that there should be more possibility of access also, because sometimes access between accused and counsel has to be procured by the security. In your case there having been no arrest warrant and no order for detention, I understand that your client does not pose any security issue. So what I would suggest you do is you move here on this side of the front row, you move further to your right; and she will sit right behind you, where she can, if necessary, be able to contact you. Is there a problem with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. Mr. Bourdon, there will be a problem with the transcript, so you can remain seated where you were, and, Ms. Hartmann, you can sit right behind Mr. Bourdon. And I also want to make clear that although I have consulted my colleagues on this already, this is the arrangement for today, I am hopeful that it is an arrangement that can continue later on, when we come to trial; but I have been unable to have a definitive answer from one of my colleagues. So that's the position for today. Having said that, I'll just introduce myself just for the record. My name is Carmel Agius, I come from the island of Malta, and I will be presiding over your initial appearance today, Madam. I want to begin by making sure that you are able to follow the proceedings, and in a language that you can understand. I know that you both understand both French and English, so I don't think the problem will arise; but if at any moment, having chosen your preferred language, you are not receiving interpretation or there is a problem with the way you are receiving interpretation, please draw my attention straight away. The same applies to you, Mr. MacFarlane, in case you're not receiving -- you're not hearing the proceedings well. Having said this, there is an important communication I wish to make at the very outset. Usually, proceedings in this Tribunal are broadcast, when they are broadcast, with a 30-minute delay. There is one exception, and that applies to initial appearances that are normally broadcast live. Earlier on today, when I was informed of the filing of a motion by you, Mr. Bourdon, on behalf of your client; and we'll be coming to that motion very shortly, I decided to order that the broadcast of this initial appearance be delayed by 30 minutes, or any other time that I will decide upon if we are not finished within 30 minutes, during which I will hear submissions from you, Mr. Bourdon, and possibly also from you, Mr. MacFarlane, and have the matter raised in the motion finally determined or resolved. Basically, the motion seeks to have my order of the 21st of October, 2008, for the release of audio-visual record and permitting photography suspended and to prohibit the taking of photographs of the respondent during today's or prior to today's initial appearance. We'll come to this shortly, as I said. In the meantime, I am confirming to you that before the sitting, I gave instructions on this matter, namely, that the usual photography session be proceeded with normally, as per my order of the 21st of October, but that no use of such photos taken be made until the matter is finally resolved after that you, Mr. Bourdon, have had a chance to make submissions on your motion. So that is the position. I am also informed on who the photographers were. They are all employed in this Tribunal, so there isn't even the need to take further precautions. Later on in these proceedings, Madam Hartmann, I will be informing you of the allegations against you; and therefore, it is important now that I inform you that you have a fundamental right, recognised by this Tribunal, namely, to remain silent throughout these and also future proceedings, and that such silence will not be held against you. Do you understand this? Okay. So we'll proceed with another formality. Today, prosecuting these proceedings is Mr. Bruce MacFarlane, amicus curiae prosecutor. He was appointed by the Deputy Registrar as far back as 3rd March 2008, and as amicus curiae investigator; and we appointed him as amicus curiae prosecutor on the 1st of September. Mr. Bourdon, you are appearing for Madam Hartmann, and you have been regularly appointed by the Registrar to represent the accused. And having said this, I suggest to give you the word now, Mr. Bourdon, to make submissions on the motion that you filed earlier on this morning. Before doing so, how much time would you require for your submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURDON
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURDON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. President, for allowing my client, Ms. Hartmann, to sit closer to me. Thank you for understanding the meaning and the significance of my motion. Indeed, we wish your decision to be stayed, the decision regarding the audio-visual record regarding the taking of photograph of Ms. Hartmann for the following reasons. These reasons have to do partly with the reasons I've already set forth in support of my motion for her to sit closer to me. I did hear what you said earlier on, Mr. President. You said and you reminded us that you believe that the offence Ms. Hartmann is charged with is of a rather serious nature. We shall return to this issue later on. But as to the taking of photographs in court, it is, in our view, something that stigmatizes -- unduly stigmatizes Ms. Florence Hartmann. Ms. Hartmann is not being charged with an offence against humanitarian law. She is not a [indiscernible]. She is a free person, and she has exerted a high-ranking position in this Tribunal. She's a person who's very respectable and very respected. She is able to take up other positions which would necessarily and naturally be of international scope, and if she were to be taken in court -- photographed in court, she would be part of a very restricted club, a circle of people who are photographed every day in such courtrooms; namely, individuals that are prosecuted for crimes against humanity. And in our view, it is not normal for Ms. Hartmann to join this club or family of people who, when they are photographed, show that they allegedly have committed crimes. But, again, we do not insist on this issue. There's nothing obsessive about it in this case, but we think it is proper and normal and totally consistent for you to stay your decision. Once again, we don't want to prevent photographers from doing their work, of course, but being photographed in court is a sign that you cannot get rid of. And in our view, it is not at all proportionate -- commensurate to the offence Ms. Hartmann is charged with. This is why, with regard to the motion I filed this morning, I humbly ask you to stay your decision by which you authorised the release, in a court setting, of photographs of Ms. Florence Hartmann. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourdon. Do you wish to comment, Mr. MacFarlane?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I disagree with my learned friend's comments with respect to the seriousness of the offence, and I to not wish to be associated with those comments. Having said that, I have given careful consideration to the motion that was filed by Mr. Bourdon, and in the circumstances I take no position on the motion, and I do not wish to make any submission with respect to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have thought about this since this morning, when I became aware of your motion, and of course I was reserving my position until I heard your submissions, in particular, Mr. Bourdon. I anticipated that Mr. MacFarlane would not take a position because it's of little concern to him. I'll try and motivate my decision as briefly as possible. You mentioned a club, and in your opinion that the ultimate result -- effect of your client being photoed, taken, immortalized, sort of, would just place her as a member of this club; but I disagree with you. The nature of the crime with which she is charged is, in itself, indicative that, if at all, she may be part of a different club; namely, a club of those who have been charged with contempt of court and not the club of those who have been charged with the obviously more serious crimes against humanity and genocide. In reading through your motion this morning, I also noticed that you extricated the element of photography from the rest, and what you are basically suggesting and requesting the Court to do is to reverse its decision, its order to have your client photographed, which is a normal procedure before this Tribunal. But you have not, as I understood your motion, asked also for the reversal of the order insofar as visual recording of proceedings is concerned, and that is a part of the essential function of this Tribunal, that all proceedings, insofar as possible, are public; they are audio-visually recorded, they are available, and in some instances they are broadcast, and in almost all instances one can also follow the proceedings on the internet by logging in the web site of this Tribunal. You have kept the two separate, while they were included in the same order. And I noticed that the reason that you gave in your motion essentially was that this violates her right for preservation of her image, that it could be prejudicial for her present and future activities, and I have seriously thought about that because I think that is at the crux of the matter. But even if I were to say, "No photographs," I think there is enough photographs of her already available on the internet that can be made use of by anyone who really wants to prejudice her current and future professional activities. And in addition -- and the fact that there will be audio-visual recordings and broadcasts of the proceedings will return us back to square 1. So even if I were to say, "No photographs," that's not going to give her any remedy or give her the remedy that she would prefer to have. I mean, such remedy would have to include also the banning of audio-visual proceedings, which is something that I am definitely not prepared to do, and there has not been one single case where that has happened. So my decision is to reject the motion, and we can therefore proceed. I will now give a summary of the indictment. Madam Hartmann, on the 27th of August of this year, a specially-appointed Chamber, over which I preside, issued an order in lieu of indictment on contempt in the case against you. Your initial appearance was scheduled and then rescheduled to the present day in two orders dated 10th and 26th September, respectively. On the 16th of October, 2008, the amicus curiae prosecutor, and I will be henceforth referring to as "the prosecutor," filed a motion to amend the order in lieu of indictment. On the 21st of October, I signed an order, as Presiding Judge, requiring you, or your counsel on your behalf, to submit a response to the motion, if at all, by the 23rd of October, 2008. In the afternoon of the 23rd of October, 2008, Mr. Bourdon informally communicated to the Chamber that there were no objections to the changes proposed in the motion. A decision on the motion, as well as an amended order in lieu of indictment, which henceforth I'll refer to as "order in lieu of indictment," were filed earlier on today. Madam Hartmann, no arrest warrant was issued in your case, and the Chamber, after consultation, also decided not to file an order for detention on remand. Since we have not ordered detention, and one reason is that we do not consider you to be a security problem, I would still request your continued cooperation with the Registry and the Tribunal's security section throughout this and also future proceedings. Madam Hartmann, I would put this question to every woman. I will be now and later referring to your year of birth. Do you want to do that in public or in private session?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I request that my address is not mentioned, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. The order in lieu of the indictment alleges that you were born in a particular year in France. Later on, I will ask you the date of birth in private session. And that you were formally employed as a spokes --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURDON
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, it's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURDON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just the address. I think the address only be mentioned in private session. Ms. Hartmann does not mind her date of birth to be mentioned. She's quite happy with her age, and it would be excessive not to mention it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. So the order in lieu of indictment alleges that you were born in 1963 in France and that you were formerly employed as spokesperson of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal. It further alleges that you authored a book for publication entitled "Paix et Chatiment," published by Flammarion on 10th September 2007; and that specific pages within that book disclosed information related to two particular decisions of the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal which had been issued and filed confidentially, one on the 20th September 2005 and the other on the 6th of April, 2006. The order in lieu of indictment alleges that in doing so, you included, and in this manner divulged, the contents and purported effect of the two particular decisions of the Appeals Chamber that I have mentioned, as well as specific reference to the confidential nature of these decisions. The order in lieu of indictment also alleges that you authored an article for publication entitled, "Vital Genocide Documents Concealed," published by the Bosnian Institute on 21st January 2008, and that the article disclosed information relating to the same two confidential decisions of the Appeals Chamber as were disclosed in your book, including the contents and purported effects of these decisions. Finally, the order in lieu of indictment alleges that in both instances, you knew that the information was confidential at the time of your alleged disclosure, you knew that the decisions from which the information was drawn were ordered to be filed confidentially; and, further, you knew that by your disclosure, you were revealing confidential information to the public. Madam Hartmann and Mr. Bourdon, you would have noticed by now that being in open session, I have not specified what the confidential Appeals Chamber decisions are about. Should it become necessary during the course of trial to go into the contents of those decisions and discuss those contents, then the Trial Chamber will move into private session so that it makes it possible for the most open discussion to take place. As a result of the allegations contained in the order in lieu of indictment, Madam Hartman, you are charged with two counts of contempt of this Tribunal, to which I will come later, punishable under this Tribunal's inherent powers and Rule 77(A)(ii) of the Rules for knowingly and willfully interfering with the administration of justice by disclosing information in violation of an order of the Appeals Chamber. That concludes my summary. I have a problem with my LiveNote, but I can proceed. It says: "Server connection disabled. Attempt to reconnect." Anyway, I don't have it at all now. Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Madam Hartmann, we now arrive -- do you wish to -- it's okay. Madam Hartmann, we arrive at the portion of your initial appearance before this Tribunal which requires, pursuant to Rule 62 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, that I inform you of the charges against you and ask you for your entry of a plea. Prior to this, however, I have a few additional questions, especially to identify you for the record. Madam Hartmann, would you please tell the Court your full name for the record? Your microphone. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Florence Hartmann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go into private session now for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Madam Hartmann, this is not just a formality, but it is something which we are keen upon. Has the embassy of -- the French Embassy, in other words, been informed of your appearance here today?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Formally, no. Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURDON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me answer for Ms. Hartmann. Officially, no, to our knowledge it has not been informed or notified officially, but informally, yes, through various channels it has been informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usually, the Tribunal does take steps to inform the relevant respective embassies. Madam Registrar, do you know if this was done in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't know. Okay, thank you. However, if you wish us to formally inform the embassy, we will do so. My information is that the embassy was informed; but again I did not ask for a formal confirmation of it. It's just information that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURDON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do not particularly wish the embassy to be informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Madam Hartmann, please make yourself comfortable. You may sit down. One of my obligations as Presiding Judge for this initial appearance is to make sure that your rights are respected today and are guaranteed for the future, when we come to trial. Articles 20 and 21 of the Statute of the Tribunal address the commencement and conduct of trial proceedings and deal with the rights of an accused. The Statute does not distinguish between accused and accused; in other words, accused of crimes against humanity and accused of contempt like we have in this case. So I am going to ask Madam Registrar to read out to you Articles 20 and 21 of our Statute.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, first I'd like to stand corrected with regards to the government of France being informed. They were informed on the 27th of August with respect to the order in lieu of an indictment on contempt. The republic was served. Article 20: "Commencement and conduct of trial proceedings." The Trial Chamber shall ensure that a trial is fair and expeditious and that proceedings are conducted in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, with full respect for the rights of the accused and due regard for the protection of victims and witnesses. A person against human indictment has been confirmed shall, pursuant to an order or an arrest warrant of the International Tribunal, be taken into custody, immediately informed of the charges against him, and transferred to the International Tribunal. The Trial Chamber shall read the indictment, satisfy itself that the rights of the accused are respected, confirm that the accused understands the indictment, and instructs the accused to enter a plea. The Trial Chamber then sets a date for trial. The hearing shall be public unless the Trial Chamber decides to close the proceedings in accordance with its Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Article 21: "Rights of the accused." All persons shall be equal before the International Tribunal. In the determination of charges against him, the accused shall be entitled to a fair and public hearing subject to Article 22 of the Statute. The accused shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to the provisions of the present Statute. In the determination of any charge against the accused pursuant to the present Statute, the accused shall be entitled to the following minimum guarantees and full equality; to be informed promptly and in detail in a which language which he understands of the nature and cause of the charge against him; to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his Defence and to communicate with counsel of his own choosing; to be tried without undue delay; to be tried in his presence and to defend himself in person or through legal assistance of his own choosing; to be informed if he does not have legal assistance of his right to have legal assistance assigned to him in any case where the interests of justice so require, and without payment by him in any such case if he does not have sufficient means to pay for it; to examine or have examined the witnesses against him and to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf under the same conditions as witnesses against him; to have the free assistance of an interpreter if he cannot understand or speak the language used in the International Tribunal; not to be compelled to testify against himself or to confess guilt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. Ms. Hartmann, do you understand the importance of these rights which were just -- which were read out to you right now, just now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish me to explain further any of these rights before we proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now we come to a stage where you have to make a choice, if you wish so. Earlier on I summarized the order in lieu of indictment. I would like to know, first of all, whether you have received a copy of the order in lieu of indictment in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you -- if you wish to consult with your lawyer, please do so. Okay. Do you understand its contents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand the allegations included in that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the charges, I suppose, as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Switch on the microphone and repeat your answer, please. Okay. Madam Hartmann, you have a right to have the order in lieu of indictment read out in its entirety to you here in open court, or you can also, instead of exercising this right, waive this right. It's your choice, and we'll do exactly as you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I waive that right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So the indictment will not be read, and we come to the question of what kind of plea you wish to enter. Pursuant to Rule 62(A)(iii) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, I am now hereby calling upon you to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty on each count in the indictment either today, or if you choose not to enter them today, within a time period that I will specify; and I have the possibility of choosing any time period within 30 days from this initial appearance. So my first question to you is whether you wish to enter a plea today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do not wish to enter a plea, and I would like my counsel to explain why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bourdon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURDON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. First of all, we want to avoid any misunderstanding. Neither Ms. Hartmann nor myself do want this -- these proceedings to last forever and needlessly, but there is a very simple practical reason why Ms. Hartmann has just taken the position you've heard. I can represent Ms. Hartmann's interests for three months because the investigations conducted in order to decide whether she can benefit from the status of indigence have not been completed, and since these investigations have not been completed, I'm not sure, Mr. President, I am not sure whether I'll have the opportunity or the pleasure to appear before you again. It may be the last time I have this opportunity. But I don't want to believe that this matter is not going to be dealt with properly. I don't want to believe that. I won't be able to be her counsel until the end of these proceedings. This is all theoretical, but the thing is that officially she has not been identified as indigent, financially speaking; and therefore she may not be able to call on me as her counsel, as such. That's why Ms. Hartmann has decided not to plead today. There is another reason. As I said, we do not want to make these proceedings last forever, but we also do not believe that there is a great deal of urgency in this matter. Let me hear -- speak under the control of Mr. MacFarlane. He got in touch with me in June, and he told me that he wanted to organise Ms. Hartmann's initial appearance as quickly as possible. I did my best to accommodate him, and I'd like to thank him for his courtesy, but there's no particular urgency in this case. A technical decision was issued this morning, I discovered it this morning, amending the indictment, and we need to have time to think in order to tell you what Ms. Hartmann's position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourdon. I fail to see the connection between the decision of the Registrar to her indigence and right for legal aid with the entering of a plea of guilty or not guilty. However, I respect your wish to defer this matter until later. Do you have an indication as to when it is likely that the Registrar will decide on the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURDON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to confess that I'm not very familiar with these types of decisions here. I have just seen on the transcript that you do not actually see the connection between the two things. I can spell it out for you. If she is not acknowledged or recognised as being indigent, I won't be able to remain her counsel, and Ms. Hartmann wants me to be her counsel. The decision taken by the accused is taken together with his or her counsel. The connection -- the link is obvious. It's very unlikely that a pragmatic solution won't be found for Ms. Hartmann in due course, but I can't tell you about the time frame, of course. But you can count on me to make everything -- to speed things up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But let me try and explain something. The Rules prescribe, in a case when the accused chooses not to plead guilty or not guilty in the course of the initial appearance, the Rules prescribe a time limit of 30 days within which then there has to be convened a further initial appearance, during which the accused will also -- will once more be asked the same question, "How do you wish to plead to the charges brought against you?" Assuming that the situation that you have raised does not crystalize and be resolved within these 30 days, the position would be that if your client repeats or maintains her position, namely, saying, "I don't wish to enter a plea," then there cannot be any further adjournments; and I would have to enter a plea of not guilty on her behalf. So I'm just mentioning this because you appear to me, like many other French lawyers that I know, a very pragmatic person; so I don't know what your client stands to gain by having this deferred to maybe another 10 days, or another 15 days, or possibly even 30 days, especially since on record she has already gone on in public saying that she will contest these proceedings. So I will ask the question again, and then if you wish me to defer this matter to later, I will certainly do so. You are adamant that you don't wish to enter a plea today?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am. I would like to wait. Today, we'll have a meeting about the matter of indigence, and I suppose that the matter will be resolved very shortly, within the next few days, once I've provided a number of documents, well within the time frame of 30 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURDON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can count on us, Your Honour. We'll do everything at our disposal to resolve matters as quickly as possible. It's not in our interest for things to go on forever. You have just mentioned the fact that Ms. Hartmann's position can be deducted by her public statements. Anyone in the press or the media can say whatever he or she likes, but it's a different matter altogether for Ms. Hartmann to state her official position before the Tribunal. It's a different matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That being so, and since, like you, Mr. Bourdon, I have no intention of letting this case prolong indefinitely, I will be issuing, in due course, a schedule for further initial appearance. My senior legal officer or the Registry will be contacting you both to see whether you have any problems with any dates, so if you can do that piece of homework straight away. My thinking is that it will be within sort of 15 days from now, something like that, but please let us know if you are unavailable on any particular day. So we can now approach the end of this initial appearance, but there are a few administrative matters that I would like to address. First, as you would have noticed from public filings in this case, the Trial Chamber composition includes, apart from me as presiding, also Judge Alphonsus Orie from the Netherlands and Judge Christine Van Den Wyngaert from Belgium. The three of us, together, will hear the case at trial. Second, it is now necessary to plan for the pre-trial activities in this case, as well as consider the schedule for the trial. In this context, you should be aware that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence for pre-trial and trial proceedings in a contempt case apply mutatis mutandis -- in ordinary case, apply mutatis mutandis to proceedings in a contempt case under Rule 77. Notwithstanding this, a Trial Chamber acting either proprio motu, or on good cause being shown by motion, pursuant to Rule 1 to 6 bis and Rule 1 to 7 respectively, as well, and I suggest that you read this, as well as the practice direction on the procedure to be applied in contempt cases, the Trial Chamber may reduce any time prescribed by or under the Rules, having regard to the complexity of the issues raised in proceedings. The raison d'etre of this is of course a matter of ensuring the expeditious administration of justice. As such, and I wish to make this clear, neither the Prosecution nor the Defence should expect to be allowed the full time specified under any particular rule of the Tribunal for such routine matters as complying with disclosure obligations, filing of motions or responses, or filing of pre-trial briefs. Where any timelines under the Rules are reduced, the parties will, of course, be informed, and the Trial Chamber will consider requests for extensions if good cause is shown. Additionally, other requirements under the Rules and directives, such as the length of pre-trial briefs to be submitted, will be reduced if we deem that to be necessary. Again, you will be informed when such reductions are thought to be fit and proper. Finally, I do not anticipate that the pre-trial stage of the proceedings will take so long as to necessitate the holding of status conferences under Rule 65 bis (a) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which would otherwise be required to be held every 120 days. If this is not the case, of course, we will have a status conference pursuant to the said Rule. Absent the possible need for a motion hearing at some point, which is a possibility, I would expect that the next time we will meet, following the further initial appearance, will be to conduct a pre-trial conference, to be followed immediately by the trial itself. Given all of these matters, let me say first to the Prosecution that I would expect you, Mr. MacFarlane, to comply with your disclosure obligations as quickly as possible, most especially the disclosure of materials supporting the orders in lieu of indictment. There is no need to take the full 30 days under Rule 66(A)(i), in my opinion. Seven days was suggested to me, but I am extending it to fourteen days from today, which would seem to be sufficient. If there are problems, if you encounter problems, you will let us know, and we'll consider granting an extension. Related to this, if you intend to file any motion necessary to carry out your disclosure obligations, you should do so immediately. And you, Mr. Bourdon, in such a case, you're kindly asked to respond as promptly as possible. I am referring to such requests as, for example, the lifting of the ex parte status of any filings prior to disclosure and also, for example, motions seeking protective measures which may accompany disclosure of confidential information to the Defence. Mr. Bourdon, I would also like to remind you of Rule 72 (a) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which allow for a 30-day period for filing any preliminary motions once you have received all the supporting material from the Prosecution. Again, I would think this could be reduced to 14 days. Given the circumstances, I would suggest, Mr. MacFarlane, that the 14 days that I have given you will start running as of today, irrespective and independently of the fact that we still don't have a plea. But the 14 days which the Defence is being granted will start running from the day of service of the documents disclosed by you, as required by our Rules. If there are problems with disclosure, Mr. Bourdon, please do contact straight away the Trial Chamber. This leads me now to a discussion -- a short, brief discussion on the date for the start of trial, and this is unless, of course, you decide, Ms. Hartmann, to plead guilty, in which case there will be no trial, as such; but there will be a sentencing hearing to be followed by judgement. But I'm assuming that you are contesting the case. Once the date for the start of trial is established, the Trial Chamber will issue a scheduling order which will include such other dates as, for example, the filing of pre-trial briefs. This will follow after the conclusion of what we refer to as the 65 ter process. I would like to hear from the parties now on when you believe it would be best to schedule the trial date. I can already inform you that, as Presiding Judge and after consultations with my colleagues, I do not foresee the trial beginning prior to the end of December of this year, so we're talking of possibly early next year. This would be based, of course, upon the schedule and availability of Judges sitting in this case. Mr. MacFarlane, do you wish to comment on this or do you have any concrete suggestions that you could make, especially since you are not residing -- both of you, you're not residing in The Hague and you have to come one from Canada and the other one from France, which is much easier?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have made special arrangements to free myself up, so I will be available to proceed to trial any time in January, February, March. Any time after December 31st, I am available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And, Mr. Bourdon, on the assumption that you will show up more than once before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURDON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would be extremely frustrated if I couldn't appear without you again -- before you again, and I would be extremely frustrated if I couldn't defend Ms. Hartmann, because it is an honour for me to defend her. I forgot to say so. I know it is a ritualistic formula, but I mean it. And you were kind enough to tell me that as far as you could remember, French lawyers were pragmatic ones, I want to pay homage to this courtesy you were kind enough to show us. I can see that there's no extreme urgency in this Tribunal, that we can provide for certain deadlines. There's one thing I would like to convey to this Tribunal, Mr. President. The prosecution of Ms. Florence Hartmann, in my view, raises issues of principle, extremely important issues of principle; and these principles and the contradiction shown therein has been a subject matter for many tribunals, as to how to reconcile these principles. I'm not sort of giving you a fore-taste of what is going to be the defence of Ms. Hartmann. I just wanted to convey to you that Ms. Hartmann's will and wish -- her will and her lawyer's wish is for the proceedings to be open and public proceedings. Why so? Just one moment, Mr. President, just half a second. Yes, the case against Ms. Hartmann raises issues of principle, that is, the duty of information, freedom of expression, and this touches to the freedom and the need for the public opinion to know how international justice operates and works. So this is the reason why I will be led to explain to you why we believe that this discussion is to be continued in the interest of the public, and for that to happen it has to be a public debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was not my question, Mr. Bourdon. My question is: What is your opinion as to the possible date of the trial, whether you agree that we're talking of early next year or -- this is basically what I am asking you to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURDON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that your question was trying to elicit a more general comment and not just an issue of scheduling. I will tell you in writing tomorrow, the day after tomorrow, when I am not available in that period as of the month of January. I know already now that the entire month of February or, basically, the entire month of February is a month when I'm not available because I'm supposed to defend another party before the Tribunal Correctionnel in Paris, and it is an important case; but I will give you my availabilities because I want it to be transparent and pragmatic, so I will tell you that without delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. This concludes all of the administrative matters I intended to raise. Prior to adjourning, Mr. MacFarlane, is there any other matter that you wish to raise at this stage before we conclude?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I believe that completes all the issues that I had anticipated today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Bourdon, is there any matter that you would like to raise at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURDON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you. No further question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Hartmann, is there any matter that you would like to raise at this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As you are both lawyers working or appearing before this Tribunal for the first time, and it's an exaltation that I make and invite you to familiarise yourself with the procedure of this Tribunal as much as possible, this is unlike any other procedure that you are used to in your domestic jurisdictions. It has got its own peculiarities, and it's very important that you familiarise yourself with them. One recent change that you may not be aware of and which I feel duty-bound to inform you about today is a recent change in the policy of the Registrar governing release of public transcripts for initial appearances. This, contrary to previous practice, requires that the parties request any change to the transcript within two working days. So please bear this in mind, should you wish to effect any changes to the public transcript of this initial appearance. I hereby adjourn the proceedings until further notice, and you will receive a communication of the date for the further initial appearance within a matter of a few days from today. Thank you.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Initial Appearance adjourned at
